item.description: 🐝 Wasps have their own biological Face ID — remarkably similar to ours. Researchers have identified specialized neurons in the brains of northern paper wasps that respond to individual facial features of other wasps. Despite having only around a million neurons, these insects use a facial recognition mechanism strikingly similar to that found in primates. It helps them maintain social hierarchies without constantly fighting. The study suggests that evolution independently developed similar neural solutions in insects and mammals, although their mechanisms are not identical. Perhaps intelligence is not just about brain size, but how efficiently neurons are organized. #Science #Neuroscience #Evolution #Biology #Intelligence https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.052

item.title: 🧬 GPT‑6 designed proteins that bind their targets OpenAI has posted a preprint:…
item.description: 🧬 GPT‑6 designed proteins that bind their targets OpenAI has posted a preprint: the GPT‑6 family designs a protein's 3D shape and its amino-acid sequence using only reasoning and ordinary code — with no specialised biology models at the generation stage. In lab tests with Onava, proteins built from GPT‑6.2's designs showed evidence of binding across five targets, and redesigned antibodies kept binding. An internal research model matched or beat specialised models on many design tasks. The authors' own caveat: the campaign relied on Boltz‑2, OpenDDE and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. The intrinsic ability is comparable to specialised models at two stages — backbone generation (RFdiffusion) and sequence redesign (ProteinMPNN) — plus a memorisation caveat in structure-to-sequence tests. This is not "AI discovered a drug". The shift is elsewhere: protein design stops being a separate discipline and becomes a task for a general-purpose model. #biotech #AI #OpenAI @science

item.title: A planet about the mass of Jupiter circles 51 Pegasi every 4.23 days. A year the…
item.description: A planet about the mass of Jupiter circles 51 Pegasi every 4.23 days. A year there is shorter than a school week. Nothing in our own system comes close. Mercury, the fastest planet here, takes 88 days; the new companion sits about eight million kilometres from its star, well inside Mercury's orbit, where a gas giant should not survive. Its temperature is above 1,300 K. The detection is a wobble, not a picture. Since April 1994 the Geneva group had been reading radial velocities of 142 G and K dwarfs to about 13 metres per second, and one star's lines slid back and forth on a 4.23-day cycle. The authors offered two readings: a giant that migrated inward, or a brown dwarf stripped of its outer layers. The search was built for stars like the Sun with planets like Jupiter in orbits like ours. It found the opposite, and the field never went back. Source: Mayor & Queloz, Nature (1995) · doi.org/10.1038/378355a0

item.title: Mathematicians are currently examining a 17-million-line proof of the Riemann Hy…
item.description: Mathematicians are currently examining a 17-million-line proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, generated with the help of Claude (consisting of 175,187 files verified using Lean and Mathlib). To make sense of the solution, they created a visualization in the form of a map—which proved to be a huge help. 😂 But I’d like everyone to consider something. Many "naive carbon-based lifeforms" still claim, "I’ll just check every single line of code the AI ​​writes." But what happens when the AI ​​dumps N million lines of code on you, and when you ask, "Bro, how does this actually work?" it replies, "Elementary, my dear Watson—here’s a visualization for you!"? 😂 Let’s be honest: trying to understand the inner workings through manual inspection is, in a sense, a dead end. A mere mortal simply cannot grasp it—at least not within any reasonable timeframe. We need formal verification methods capable of handling this level of complexity to ensure correctness. Mathematicians at least have Lean—a formal tool for verification. Similar tools are also needed for business software, where logic is often fuzzy. Yet, by 2027, we could easily end up with a "superintelligent jellyfish" of code—the result of letting a swarm of AI agents run wild. bosnadev.com/lab/riemann/app

item.title: Cold fusion's neutrons arrived 10¹² times too few to explain its heat. In 1989 M…
item.description: Cold fusion's neutrons arrived 10¹² times too few to explain its heat. In 1989 Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons ran a current through heavy water between palladium electrodes, measured more heat leaving than the current put in, and called the cause nuclear fusion of deuterium. Fusion that released that much heat would also release neutrons, at a rate fixed by the same reaction. Counters found nothing near it. A Department of Energy panel that visited the labs that year put the yield "at levels 10¹² below the amounts required to explain the experiments claiming excess heat". The fault was structural. The claim could not fail: a cell that gave heat proved it, a cell that gave none was called faulty. No retraction followed. A result that cannot fail is not a result, however hot the glass gets. Second source: US DOE ERAB, Cold Fusion Research (1989) · osti.gov/biblio/5144772 Source: Fleischmann & Pons, J. Electroanal. Chem. (1989) · doi.org/10.1016/0022-0728(89)80006-3

item.title: About 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth — and they outweigh every wild bird and …
item.description: About 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth — and they outweigh every wild bird and mammal. Ants are everywhere, yet until recently nobody had a defensible estimate of how many there are. Six researchers pooled 489 studies from every continent and major biome — forest floor, canopy, desert — and scaled the samples up to the whole planet. Their conservative figure: more than 3 × 10¹⁵ ants live on the ground, and close to 20 × 10¹⁵ in total. Dried out, that is about 12 megatons of carbon: more than the combined biomass of all wild birds and mammals, and roughly a fifth of the carbon in humanity. The distribution is wildly uneven. Numbers peak in the tropics and vary widely between habitats; leaf-litter ants are densest in forests, active foragers in arid land. The authors call ants a central part of terrestrial ecosystems — and note that you cannot track a group whose size was never measured. Source: Schultheiss et al., PNAS 119, e2201550119 (2022) · doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2201550119

item.title: Rutherford's gold atom needed 100 positive charges in a single point. Before 191…
item.description: Rutherford's gold atom needed 100 positive charges in a single point. Before 1911 the atom was a soft ball: positive charge spread evenly through a sphere the size of the atom, electrons embedded in it. An alpha particle fired at that ball should be nudged gently by the diffuse charge. Almost none should come back. Rutherford took the ones that did and worked backwards. To turn an alpha particle around, the repulsive field has to be strong, and a spread-out charge cannot supply it. Put the charge at the centre. With 100 e there, an alpha particle at 2.09 × 10⁹ cm per second is brought to rest 3.4 × 10⁻¹² cm from that centre, while the atom's own radius is 10⁻⁸ cm. That gap is the result. The distance at which the alpha is stopped is roughly three thousand times smaller than the atom's own radius, and the space between is empty. The ball became a point. The point kept the charge. Source: Rutherford, Philosophical Magazine (1911) · doi.org/10.1080/14786440508637080

item.title: 🐢 A 194-year-old tortoise is revealing how to age slowly Jonathan, an Aldabra g…
item.description: 🐢 A 194-year-old tortoise is revealing how to age slowly Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise believed to have hatched in 1832, is the oldest known living land animal. In a study published in Science Advances, researchers found his epigenome — the system controlling which genes are on or off — has remained strikingly stable, with DNA repair and metabolism controls resembling those of much younger tortoises. His longevity is not just inherited genes; his body has also avoided some age-related genetic changes. The team identified 287 distinctive genetic variants tied to protection against aging, influencing DNA repair, inflammation, insulin activity, and cancer suppression. It is the first epigenome study of a giant tortoise, and longevity in humans is far from proven here. #tortoise #longevity #genetics @science

item.title: 🛰 BepiColombo is in orbit around Mercury — only the second mission ever On 21 N…
item.description: 🛰 BepiColombo is in orbit around Mercury — only the second mission ever On 21 November at 18:24 UTC four thrusters on ESA's MPO module burned for 37 minutes, slowing the stack enough for Mercury's weak gravity to capture it. Confirmation reached Darmstadt about 3.5 hours later, after telemetry analysis. The cruise took eight years and some 10 billion km: flybys of Earth, Venus twice, Mercury six times. Launch: October 2018, Kourou. ⏳ On 9–10 December ESA's MPO and JAXA's Mio separate and head for their own orbits. Science starts on 6 April 2027 and runs at least a year. 🔎 Targets: surface composition and geology, the oversized iron core, the magnetic field and its coupling to the solar wind, plus water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters. Only NASA's MESSENGER (2011–2015) orbited Mercury before; no mission has run two spacecraft there at once. 💬 "Mercury is the terrestrial planet we know least about," says ESA's Geraint Jones. Ill.: ESA/ATG medialab #space #Mercury #BepiColombo @science
